title: My God, Thy Service Well Demands
description: My God, Thy Service Well Demands in Tonic Solfa to CAITHNESS, doh is D: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 5 verses and a piano.
about: Philip Doddridge wrote these words. They were printed in Hymns for Christian Devotion, compiled by John G. Adams and Edwin H. Chapin (Boston, 1846), as hymn 932 of its twenty-second edition (1853), “Sickness and Recovery”.
The book printed the words without tunes, marked Common Metre (8.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to CAITHNESS; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.
underlay: My God, thy ser-vice well de-mands The rem-nant of my days; Why was this fleet-ing breath re-newed, But to re-new thy praise?

lines: My God, thy service well demands
The remnant of my days;
Why was this fleeting breath renewed,
But to renew thy praise?
Thine arms of everlasting love
Did this weak frame sustain,
When life was hovering o'er the grave,
And nature sunk with pain.
I calmly bowed my fainting head
On thy dear, faithful breast,
And waited for my Father's call
To his eternal rest.
Back from the borders of the grave,
At thy command, I come;
Nor will I ask a speedier flight
To my celestial home.
Where thou appointest mine abode
There would I choose to be;
For in thy presence death is life,
And earth is heaven with thee.

licence: Public domain: Philip Doddridge died in 1751.
credits: Words by Philip Doddridge (1702–1751), public domain, as printed in Hymns for Christian Devotion (1853); set to CAITHNESS by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
